opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting directions, but I'd frame it a bit differently from how people usually talk about it.

Right now, most of our AI systems live inside a chat box. They wait for you to type something, then they respond. All the intelligence is reactive and text-mediated. But humans don't experience the world that way. We're continuously perceiving: seeing, hearing, moving through space. Most of what we know about the world never gets written down in language at all. So if you want an AI that actually understands your world, not just the internet's description of the world, it needs to be there with you, perceiving continuously. Wearables, like glasses, are the natural form factor for that because they share your first-person perspective.

The world model part is what makes it more than just a camera strapped to your face. A world model, in the sense I care about, is a system that builds an internal representation of the environment: what objects are where, how things move, what's likely to happen next, what the consequences of an action would be. If you have that running on an always-on device, the assistant isn't just answering "what is this thing in front of me?" It can remember that you put your keys on the kitchen counter two hours ago. It can notice you're about to make a mistake while cooking or assembling something. It can anticipate what you need before you ask. That's a qualitatively different kind of intelligence: grounded, spatial, temporal, and personal.

I'd also say there's a feedback loop that matters a lot for research. Today's vision models are trained mostly on curated internet images and videos, which are very biased: third-person, aesthetically framed, edited. Continuous egocentric data is much closer to how a child learns. So these devices could become not just a product, but a way for models to learn from the real world in a much richer way.

That said, I don't want to sound overly utopian. There are hard problems. Technically, running real perception and memory continuously under tight power and compute budgets is very difficult; you need efficient representations, not just giant models in the cloud. And then there's privacy, which I think is the real bottleneck. An always-on device sees your life, and also the lives of everyone around you. If we don't get the trust part right, with on-device processing, clear user control, and social norms, the technology won't be accepted, and honestly it shouldn't be.

But in the long run, I believe the path to AI that truly understands the physical world goes through embodiment of some kind, whether that's robots or devices that share our perspective. Wearables might be the first place most people actually experience a world model in their daily life.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the potential is enormous, but it's mostly latent right now, because we don't yet have the thing that would make it work.

Let me explain what I mean. If you put a camera and a microphone on someone's glasses and leave it on all day, you're collecting something no dataset on the internet has: continuous, first-person, embodied experience. Hours and hours of someone walking into a kitchen, picking up a cup, having a conversation, getting interrupted, looking for their keys. The web is full of text and curated images and edited video. It has almost none of this. So from a pure research perspective, always-on wearables are the most interesting data source we've ever had access to.

But here's the catch. A language model is not the right engine for that stream. Language is a compressed, lossy summary of the world that humans already did the work of abstracting. The raw sensory stream is not compressed. It's redundant, it's noisy, most of it is boring, and the interesting parts are about physical state: where things are, what's about to happen, what changed since I last looked. That's what a world model is supposed to capture. A model that learns to predict how the scene evolves, that builds some internal representation of objects and space and causality, rather than just captioning frames.

If you have that, then the wearable stops being a recording device and becomes something closer to a second attention. It can notice that you left the stove on, not because you asked, but because it has a model of the stove and of you walking away. It can remember where you put something because it tracked the object, not because it transcribed a sentence. It can anticipate, which is the thing current assistants fundamentally cannot do. They react to queries. A world model running continuously could act on expectations.

Now, what I'd push back on is the idea that this is close. We have very good video generation now, and people sometimes conflate that with world models. Generating a plausible-looking clip is not the same as maintaining a consistent, persistent understanding of a real environment over hours. The representation problem is still open. I actually think we've over-invested in the generative side and under-invested in the question of what the right internal representation is for understanding, and wearables will expose that gap very quickly, because the real world doesn't let you cheat.

The other part I'd be careful about is that always-on is a social and privacy question before it's a technical one. If the model has to ship every frame to a server, this doesn't work, both because of latency and because nobody should want that. So the architecture almost has to be local, efficient, and selective about what it keeps. That's actually a nice forcing function. It pushes you toward models that learn to compress experience into something useful rather than hoarding pixels, which is also what a good world model should do anyway.

So, to sum up: I think it's one of the most promising directions in AI, specifically because it's the application that would finally demand real world models instead of letting us get by with language and retrieval. But I'd say we're at the beginning. The data is about to exist. The models that can actually use it are still being figured out.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is an AI that shares your context over time. When you ask a question today, you usually have to explain what you’re looking at, what you’re doing, and what happened before. An always-on wearable could have some of that context already, so the interaction becomes much more natural.

World models could help it go beyond recognizing what’s in front of the camera. Ideally, it would understand how a situation is changing, anticipate what might happen next, and connect that to what you’re trying to do. If you’re assembling something, for example, it could notice that you missed a step and help before you get stuck.

But understanding the world and knowing when to intervene are different problems. You don’t want something constantly narrating your life. It needs to recognize uncertainty, know when to ask, and often just stay quiet. And with an always-on device, privacy and control have to be fundamental: what gets remembered, what gets processed locally, and how you account for the people around you.

So I see a lot of potential, but the goal shouldn’t simply be to capture more data. It should be to turn shared context into useful help, with very little effort from the person wearing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is to move from an AI that you explicitly ask questions to an AI that understands the context in which you’re asking them. A wearable could see what you’re seeing, hear what you’re hearing, and maintain some memory of what has happened. Then you don’t have to explain everything from scratch every time you need help.

A world model could make that more useful by helping the system understand how a situation evolves—what might happen next, or what might change if you take a particular action. Imagine you’re trying to fix something. The system could follow the process with you, recognize that a step didn’t work, and update its suggestion.

But always-on perception alone isn’t enough. The hard part is deciding what matters, what to remember, and when to speak. An assistant that constantly interrupts you would be exhausting. It also needs to recognize uncertainty, and you need control over what it records and retains.

So I see a lot of potential, but the goal should be useful assistance with very little friction. Sometimes the most intelligent thing the device can do is stay quiet.
